title: One positron, a speck of antimatter, was kept for months without ever touching a wall
body: In October 2026 physicist Gerald Gabrielse’s group at Northwestern University reported a “one-positron quantum cyclotron”, accepted in Physical Review Letters ([preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08147)). A positron is the electron’s antimatter twin: the same mass, the opposite charge, and it is destroyed in a flash of gamma rays as soon as it touches ordinary matter. So it floats in a vacuum inside a **Penning trap**. A 5.6-tesla magnet bends its motion into tight circles, about 156 billion turns a second, so it cannot drift sideways, and charged electrodes at both ends push it back, so instead of sliding out along the field it bounces to and fro about 206 million times a second. Cooled to 0.3 degrees above absolute zero, its circling settles into the lowest quantum state, and microwaves can lift it one level at a time. Next the team wants to measure the positron’s tiny magnetism as precisely as the electron’s, known to 1 part in 10 trillion. Theory says the two must be exactly equal, so any difference would break a basic symmetry of physics, CPT.

slides.prompt: A positron is destroyed the instant it touches ordinary matter. So how can a lab keep one for months?
slides.answer: Float it in a vacuum, held only by magnetic and electric fields
slides.detail: A Penning trap: a strong magnet stops it drifting sideways and charged end caps stop it sliding out. Nothing solid ever touches it.

slides.alt: Animation in a cold teal lab. An electron and a positron side by side; a positron hits a wall and flashes into gamma rays. In a Penning trap the positron circles in a magnet, slides out along the field, and copper end caps bounce it back. It cools to the lowest energy level; microwaves lift it.

slides.prompt: Set the magnet and the voltage on the end caps of a Penning trap. Keep the positron away from every wall for the whole run.
slides.takeaway: Both are needed: no voltage and it slides out; too much and it spirals into the ring. It holds when circling beats bouncing by over 1.41 times. In the real trap: 757 times.

slides.heading: Catching one
slides.text: Physicist Gerald Gabrielse’s team at Northwestern University in the US takes positrons from a weak radioactive sodium-22 source and slows them in a crystal of tungsten, so that the trap can catch one. Loading a positron takes 8 to 11 hours, but once caught, a single one has stayed trapped for months.

left.label: Electron
left.text: Its magnetism is known to 1 part in 10 trillion, measured with a single electron in the same kind of trap.

right.label: Positron
right.text: The team’s next goal: the same precision. Theory says the two must be exactly equal.

slides.question: In a Penning trap, what stops the positron sliding out along the magnetic field?
slides.explanation: The magnet only stops it drifting sideways. Charged end caps push the positron back towards the middle, so it bounces to and fro about 206 million times a second.
